_comment: Shahnama of Firdausi, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II: Kai Kaus tempted; White Div's blindness; Seven Courses 1-4. Paraphrase passages with notes.

title.en: A Div in Minstrel's Guise Tempts Kai Kaus

region.zh: 卡烏斯樂宮（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus secs. 2-3

summary.en: Sipping wine on a crystal-footed throne, Kai Kaus boasts that no Shah is worthy but himself — and a div in a minstrel's guise is admitted to sing of Mazandaran, its ever-blooming gardens and rose-water rivers. Enchanted, the Shah resolves to lead a host against the land of the divs; the nobles turn pale, send in haste to Zal, and Zal comes to counsel: that land is the home of warlock-divs and under spells which none hath power to loose. The Shah answers that he in courage, Grace, and treasure surpasses Jamshid and Faridun, and Zal, baffled, takes his leave with both sun and moon darkened in his eyes.
summary.zh: 卡烏斯坐於水晶足御座上飲酒自誇「無王配此座」，一名魔化樂師獲准入宮，彈唱馬贊德蘭的四季花園與玫瑰香河。王心醉神迷，決意征討魔國；群臣變色，急遣使請扎勒進諫：「那是術士魔怪的老巢，咒術無人能解。」王卻自稱勇武天恩勝過賈姆希德與法里東。扎勒無奈告退，眼中日月俱暗。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Kaus, succeeding to his father's throne with all the world to serve him, sat one day and quaffed delicious wine within a pleasure-palace arabesqued with gold, on the golden throne whose feet were crystal, master of the world, and spake on this wise: who is Shah but I, who worthy of the throne except myself? I rule the world with none to say me nay.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Shah was thus conversing in his cups, what while the captains wondered, when a div in minstrel's guise addressed the chamberlain: a native of Mazandaran am I, a noted bard. When his harp was tuned he sang a ditty of Mazandaran: may I forget my native land never; on its heights the hyacinth and tulip bloom, there is neither heat nor cold, but spring is ever present; as for the rivers thou wouldst say they run rose-water surely.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The words roused Kai Kaus, who resolved to lead a host against Mazandaran, and harangued his warriors: we have been too fond of feast; in fortune, Grace, and birth I pass Jamshid, Zahhak, and Kai Kubad, and must surpass them in prowess too. The nobles heard and liked it not, turned pale, and frowned, for no one wished to fight the divs, though daring not to say so openly; they met thereafter and sent a cameleer in haste to Zal: if now thy head be soiled stay not to wash it, but whet thy wits and let us see thy face.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus secs. 2-3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Zal, attended by the lords, counselled the Shah: none of thy mighty predecessors thought of such a journey; Mazandaran is the home of warlock-divs and under spells which none hath power to loose; so give not thou men, wealth, and money to the winds. Kaus replied: nathless I in courage, Grace, and treasure surpass Jamshid and Faridun; I shall go thither, snare them all, then tax them heavily or leave all dead. Zal heard, and baffled answered: thou art Shah, and we are slaves who must move and breathe according to thy will; no one can root out death or sew up the eyes of destiny with needles. Grieved that the Shah would go, Zal took his leave in haste, and as he left the monarch's presence both sun and moon were darkened in his eyes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus secs. 3-4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The White Div's Tent of Pitchy Smoke

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus sec. 4

summary.en: Giv leads two thousand mace-wielders into Mazandaran, sacking and burning cities, and the Shah marvels at a land like Paradise. But the monarch of Mazandaran summons the White Div, who rises like a mountain, head level with the turning sky, spreads above the Iranian host a tent of pitchy smoke, and showers stones and darts from the sky. When day had come the ambitious Shah and most among his warriors were blind, his troops were prisoners, and his treasures pillaged: I was to blame for this, moans Kaus, and I alone.
summary.zh: 吉夫率兩千持錘武士蹂躪馬贊德蘭，燒殺擄掠；卡烏斯嘆此地如天堂。然而馬贊德蘭王急召白魔——其身如山、頂天立地——向伊朗軍頭頂張起黑煙之幕，自天撒下石鏢。天明時，驕狂之王與大部分將士皆盲，部眾被擄、財寶被劫。卡烏斯哀嘆：「此禍唯我一人之過。」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Warner identifies the White Div with the white daevas of the Avestan Dinkard tradition. No living community restriction.

passages.text: At dawn they woke and entered helmed and armed the presence of the Shah, who ordered Giv: choose from the warriors two thousand men, mace-wielders, to prepare for us a path Mazandanin-ward, slaughter young and old, fire all the settlements, turn day to night, and slay the warlocks ere they are aware. Giv girt him, reached Mazandaran, showered scimitars and maces; the women, children, and old men with staves received no quarter from his sword; he sacked and burned the cities.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He lighted on a spot like Paradise, replete with all delights: the cattle were past count. They told Kaus the news, who cried: happy the man who said Mazandaran may match with Paradise. The Iranians plundered for one week, then ceased. The monarch of Mazandaran received the news; his heart was sad, his head was heavy, and there was a div named Sanja at the court, to whom the monarch said: go and tell the White Div there hath come a host out of Iran to spoil Mazandaran; without thy help we shall be all destroyed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The White Div answered: be not in despair, for I am coming with a mighty host to cut the Shah's foot from Mazandaran. He spake and like a mountain rose erect, his head level with the turning sky. Night came, a cloud involved the Iranian host, and the world grew like a negro's face for blackness. The White Div spread above their heads a tent of pitchy smoke; from the sky he showered stones and darts; the Iranian troops dispersed abroad, and many sought Iran heart-broken at the doings of Kaus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: When day had come the ambitious Shah and most among his warriors were blind. The nobles were wroth with him, his troops were prisoners, his treasures pillaged, and his fortunes old. Now when the Shah perceived his plight he said: a prudent minister is more than treasure; alas that I accepted not the counsel of Zal the worldlord but misdoubted it. The White Div went back to his home as glorious as the sun, while Kai Kaus remained within Mazandaran to moan: I was to blame for this and I alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The First Course: Rakhsh Fights the Lion While Rustam Sleeps
title.zh: 七關之一：拉赫什獅口搏命

region.en: Onager plain en route to Mazandaran (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 赴馬贊德蘭途中野驢平原（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus sec. 6 (First Course)

summary.en: Rustam makes a two days' journey into one, catches an onager with his royal lasso, roasts and eats it, slips off Rakhsh's bridle, and sleeps in a reed-bed that is fear's own door, for a lion's lair is in it. The lion resolves to maim the steed first; Rakhsh rages like fire, lashes out at its head, fixes his teeth in its back, and dashes the beast to pieces. Rustam wakes and scolds the foolish Rakhsh: hadst thou perished, could I have carried my helmet, tiger-skin, bow, lasso, sword, and massive mace to Mazandaran?
summary.zh: 魯斯塔姆兩日併作一日趕路，以套索獵野驢炙食，解下拉赫什韁繩，睡於蘆葦叢——那正是獅子的巢穴。獅子先撲駿馬；拉赫什如烈火般反抗，咬住獅背將其撕碎。英雄醒來斥責「愚馬」：你若死了，我怎能把頭盔虎皮弓索刀錘帶往馬贊德蘭？

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; first of the Haft Khan episodes. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Rustam, that world-brightening paladin, departed from his sire and, treating night like day, made two days' journey into one, not giving Rakhsh repose. Now as his body failed him through lack of food he reached a plain where onager abounded, and the Lion with his royal lasso caught a gallant onager and, striking sparks upon an arrow's point, enkindled fire with stubble, thorns, and wood to roast the beast; he ate the flesh and threw away the bones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He spied some pasture, slipped off Rakhsh's bridle, turned him out loose upon the meadow-land, and made himself a couch within a reed-bed; he deemed it safe though it was fear's own door, for in it was a lion's lair. One watch passed, then the lion came boldly forth and was amazed to see an elephantine form among the reeds, reposing with a charger standing by. First, said the lion, I must maim the steed, then I can take the rider when I please.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He sprang at glossy Rakhsh, who raged like fire and lashed out at the lion's head, then fixed his sharp teeth in its back and dashed the beast to pieces by a shift that made it shiftless. When Rustam, deft of hand, awoke and saw how earth was straitened to that ravening beast he said: O foolish Rakhsh! who bade thee fight a lion? Hadst thou perished 'neath its claws could I have carried to Mazandaran my helmet, tiger-skin, bow, lasso, sword, and massive mace? He slept and rested long, and when the sun rose o'er the darksome hills awoke still drowsy, rubbed down Rakhsh and saddled him, then prayed to God, the Author of all good, for aid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Second Course: The Ram that Led to Water

region.zh: 赴馬贊德蘭途中焦漠（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus sec. 7 (Second Course)

summary.en: Rustam faces a waterless desert of intense heat that dried the birds to powder; his tongue fails, and the elephantine form falls on the burning dust. A well-fed ram passes by; the hero follows it till he sees the spring, and looking toward heaven says: the ram hath left no tracks about the spring — it is no desert-sheep of flesh and blood. He blesses the ram that rescued Rustam, roasts an onager, charges Rakhsh to fight nothing, and sleeps.
summary.zh: 魯斯塔姆陷入酷熱無水的荒漠，飛鳥成灰；他舌焦唇裂，如象之軀轟然倒於滾燙沙土。一頭肥羊經過；英雄強撑追隨至泉邊，仰望上蒼：「泉邊無羊蹄印——此非凡俗之羊！」他祝福引路的羊，烤食野驢，命拉赫什不得擅鬥，然後安然入睡。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the ram is read as a divine provision. No living community restriction.

passages.text: He had to face, all dizzy as he was, a desert waterless, a heat intense that dried the birds to powder; plain and waste were as they had been scorched. Rakhsh was exhausted, while his rider's tongue failed through the heat and drought, and Rustam, clutching a double-headed dart, went staggering like one bemused, and saw no means of safety. He looked up saying: O all-righteous Judge! Thou bring'st all toil and hardship on my head; I fare in hope that God will grant deliverance to the Shah, and that the Ruler of the world will free the Iranians from the clutches of the Div.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: This said, that elephantine form became weak and distraught with thirst, and fell, with tongue all cracked and blistered, on the burning dust. Anon a well-fed ram passed by. The hero on seeing thought: where is its watering-place? In sooth God's mercy is extended to me! Then in the Worldlord's strength he rose to his feet and followed up the ram until he saw the spring, for thither went that stately ram. Then Rustam looked toward heaven and said: the ram hath left no tracks about the spring! It is no desert-sheep of flesh and blood!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He blessed that ram and said: ne'er may mishap from circling heaven be thine; green be thy pastures; may cheetah never mark thee for its prey; snapped be the bow and dark the soul of him that shooteth at thee who hath rescued Rustam. His praises offered he unsaddled Rakhsh, washed him, and made him shining as the sun. Then Rustam much refreshed filled up his quiver, roasted an onager, feasted, and said to Rakhsh: fight not and make no friends; if any foe approacheth run to me, but venture not to counter divs and lions. He lay and slept, his lips in silence bound.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 7 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Third Course: Rustam and the Dragon of the Waste

region.zh: 赴馬贊德蘭途中魔地（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus sec. 8 (Third Course)

summary.en: A dragon comes from the waste whose haunt no div dared pass: no lions, divs, or elephants that went that way escaped its clutches. Rakhsh thrice rouses his sleeping master — and is twice chidden for it, threatened with the scimitar — till the Maker wills that the dragon be seen. The dragon boasts centuries of possession; Rustam names himself son of Zal and lays its head in dust, Rakhsh joining the fray, biting at its shoulders and tearing its hide; blood jets out in rivers, and the carcase hides the earth.
summary.zh: 荒漠巨龍現身——此地連魔怪也不敢擅越。拉赫什三度喚醒沉睡的主人，兩度遭斥，險些被劍斬首；直到造物主令龍現形。巨龍誇口盤踞數百年，魯斯塔姆自報家門「扎勒之子」，與龍搏鬥；拉赫什咬其肩、撕其皮，利劍斬下龍首，血如江河，龍屍蔽野。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; second Shahnama dragon-slaying of Rustam (cf. persian-sam-dragon-kashaf). No living community restriction.

passages.text: A dragon, such an one as no elephant could 'scape, came from the waste. Its haunt was there; no div dared pass thereby. It came, beheld the atheling asleep, a charger near him, and was wroth. It thought: what do I see? Who dareth to sleep here? Because no lions, divs, or elephants dared pass that way or, if they did, escaped not the clutches of that dragon fierce and fell, it turned on glossy Rakhsh, who ran to Rustam, stamped with his brazen hoofs upon the ground, whisked with his tail, and gave a thundering neigh.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The hero woke up furious, perceived not that fell dragon, and wreaked his wrath on Rakhsh for waking him. He slept again; again the worm approached out of the gloom; Rakhsh ran to Rustam's couch and kicked the earth about. Thou canst not blink the darkness of the night, said the sleeper, yet wakest me again impatiently! If thou disturb me more I will behead thee with my sharp scimitar. Then for the third time with his tiger-skin upon his breast he set himself to sleep. The fearsome dragon roared and, thou hadst said, breathed fire; Rakhsh, o'ermastered by affection for his lord, rushed to Rustam's side and pawed upon the ground, till the Maker willed that the dragon should be seen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Rustam unsheathed the keen sword at his girdle, thundered out like spring-clouds, and filled earth with battle-fire. Tell thy name, said he to the dragon; earth is no longer thine. The laidly dragon said: none escapeth me; for centuries this waste hath been my home, and mine its firmament; no eagle dareth to fly across or star to dream thereof. I am Rustam, he answered, sprung from Zal, the son of Sam and Nariman withal. The dragon closed with him, and Rakhsh, on seeing its might, laid his ears back, joined the fray, bit at the dragon's shoulders and tore its hide as though he were a lion; the paladin with keen glaive smote off the dragon's head, blood jetted out in rivers, and its carcase hid the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fourth Course: The Witch in the Lasso

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Kai Kaus sec. 9 (Fourth Course)

summary.en: Rustam comes upon a desert laid out like a banquet-hall — a spring bright as pheasant's eyes, a golden bowl of wine, a roasted mountain-sheep, and a dainty lute — and sings to it of his toils: 'tis dragon, div, and desert, one perpetual engagement. The sound reaches a witch's ears; she makes her cheeks like spring and sits down by him, but when he names the Giver of all good her favour changes, she blackens at God's name, and Rustam, flinging his lasso quicker than the wind, ensnares a fetid hag all guile and wrinkle and cleaves her with his blade.
summary.zh: 魯斯塔姆行至術士布置的宴場——清泉、金盃美酒、烤羊與豎琴——彈唱自況：「終日所對者，唯龍、魔與荒漠。」琴聲入巫耳，巫女敷粉扮春，坐於其側；魯斯塔姆一念「施恩之神」之名，她容色驟變、聞神名而獰。英雄疾擲套索，套住一個滿面皺紋的醜巫，揮劍斬之。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Thanksgivings done, he harnessed rose-cheeked Rakhsh and mounting came in time where sorcerers dwelt. Long had he fared and saw, as Sol declined, trees, grass, and stream, the very spot for youth. There was a spring as bright as pheasant's eyes; beside it were a golden bowl of wine, a roasted mountain-sheep with bread thereon, and salts and sweetmeats. Rustam thanked the Lord for showing him a place so opportune. It was a sorcerers' meal, and when he came his voice had caused those divs to disappear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 9 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He sat beside the rushy stream, brimmed a jewelled cup with wine, took up the lute, touched the chords, and sang: Oh! Rustam is an outcast still and hath no days of pleasure; his combatings are never done; 'tis dragon, div, and desert, one perpetual engagement. The sound of music reached a witch's ears; she made her cheeks like spring, although by rights she was not fair, and then, perfumed and decked, approached, saluted, and sat down by Rustam.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 9 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Not knowing that she was a wicked witch, an Ahriman beneath her bravery, he handed her a cup of wine, invoking the Giver of all good. Now when he named the Lord of love her favour changed; no soul had she for gratitude, no tongue for praise, but blackened at God's name, while Rustam, flinging his lasso quicker than the wind, ensnared her, and questioned her: what art thou? Speak and show thy proper favour. In the lasso's coils there was a fetid hag all guile and wrinkle, calamitous. He clave her with his blade and made the hearts of sorcerers afraid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Kaus sec. 9 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
